scenes.tts: Dead bacteria changed living ones into their own type. What was passed across? In 1928, living harmless bacteria were mixed with heat-killed deadly ones and injected into mice. Some mice died. From them came living bacteria of the dead strain's type, and they bred true.
scenes.visual: Two groups of cells with a yellow question mark between; mixing turns the living cells to the dead cells' type, and the change is kept.
scenes.narration: Dead bacteria changed living ones into their own type. What was passed across? In 1928, living harmless bacteria were mixed with heat-killed deadly ones and injected into mice. Some mice died. From them came living bacteria of the dead strain's type, and they bred true.

scenes.tts: Later, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty purified the active fraction and tried enzymes on it. Trypsin and chymotrypsin break down protein. Activity stayed. Ribonuclease breaks down R N A. Activity stayed. An enzyme preparation that breaks down DNA destroyed it. They called the agent principally, if not solely, DNA. A protein below their detection limit could not be ruled out.
scenes.visual: Three activity bars, one per enzyme; the DNA-digesting enzyme drops its bar to zero.

scenes.tts: Phage T2 is little more than a protein coat around DNA. Protein holds sulfur. DNA holds none, but is rich in phosphorus. So Hershey and Chase labelled the protein with sulfur thirty-five. Phosphorus thirty-two labelled mostly the DNA. They let the phage attach to E. coli, then sheared it off in a blender. About seventy-five percent of the sulfur came off. Only about fifteen percent of the phosphorus did. The stripped cells still made phage. Those progeny carried less than one percent of the parental sulfur, and thirty percent or more of the parental phosphorus. This did not prove that no protein entered.
scenes.visual: A phage with coat and DNA labelled by two tracers, sheared off a bacterium, then bars for the fluid and for the progeny.
scenes.caption: Phage T2 is little more than a protein coat around DNA. Protein holds sulfur. DNA holds none, but is rich in phosphorus. So Hershey and Chase labelled the protein with sulfur-35. Phosphorus-32 labelled mostly the DNA. They let the phage attach to E. coli, then sheared it off in a blender. About 75% of the sulfur came off. Only about 15% of the phosphorus did. The stripped cells still made phage. Those progeny carried less than 1% of the parental sulfur, and 30% or more of the parental phosphorus. This did not prove that no protein entered.

scenes.tts: Then came the structure. Two chains coil together and run in opposite directions. Adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine. So in double-stranded DNA the amounts match. If a sample is twenty-two percent adenine, thymine is also twenty-two. That leaves fifty-six percent for guanine and cytosine, so each is twenty-eight.
scenes.visual: A letter duplex with pairs lit in turn, then base-percentage bars worked from 22 percent A.

scenes.tts: Because pairing is specific, one strand fixes the sequence of the other. Watson and Crick proposed that the two chains separate, and each serves as a template for a new partner. Think of each strand as a photographic negative of the other. Print from each, and you get two copies of the original pair.
scenes.visual: The duplex splits; new green letters build a partner on each old strand, giving two duplexes.

scenes.tts: That was a proposal, not a test. In 1958, Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli on heavy nitrogen, then moved it to light nitrogen. They separated the DNA by density. After one generation, all the DNA was hybrid. After two, hybrid and light DNA were present in equal amounts. That is what templating predicts. When strands pair by rule, one strand tells you the other, and a gene can be copied.
scenes.visual: Three centrifuge tubes: one heavy band, one hybrid band, then equal hybrid and light bands.
